title: Baizhang's rake
hook: old Baizhang keeps working; when his tools are hidden, he doesn't eat

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mazu, who said this very mind is Buddha, and later turned it upside down. Your line was this very mind. Where did you catch your own mind at work? Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

Morning in a Chinese mountain monastery, and the monks are heading out to the fields with hoes and rakes. Walking among them, slowly, is their teacher. He is old now, and the monks are worried about him. They have asked him to rest. He keeps coming anyway. So one night they do the only thing they can think of. They hide his tools. The next morning the teacher looks for them, finds nothing, and goes back to his room. At mealtime his bowl stays empty. He doesn't eat. Not that day, the story says, and not until the tools come back. His name was Baizhang, a student of Mazu, and today we follow him out to the field.
screen: `AN OLD TEACHER IN THE FIELDS.` → `THE MONKS HIDE HIS TOOLS.` → `THE BOWL STAYS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: First, what he said. When the monks asked why he wouldn't eat, the story has Baizhang answer with a short line, and it is the line he is remembered for: a day without work is a day without food. Your line comes from it. No work, no food. Second, what it is not. This isn't a boss counting hours, and it isn't a rule that people who can't work go hungry. Nobody was asking more of an old man. Baizhang asked it of himself. The work in the field was part of the practice, the same as the sitting and the chanting, and he would not be left out of it because of his age. Third, the community. Tradition credits Baizhang with shaping the rules for Chan monasteries, where everyone, teacher included, took a share of the daily labor: hauling water, cutting wood, working the fields. Later monastic codes carried his name. How much of the written code goes back to him is uncertain, so treat the details as tradition. The picture holds, though. In this kind of monastery, awakening was not only on the cushion. It was also at the end of a rake. Fourth, why the tools matter. The monks hid them out of love. Baizhang didn't scold anyone. He simply would not be excused from the practice. Sweeping, planting, washing the bowl: done fully, any of it can be the whole of the path for that hour.
screen: `A DAY WITHOUT WORK, A DAY WITHOUT FOOD.` · `ASKED OF HIMSELF, NOT OF OTHERS.` · `EVERYONE WORKS, TEACHER INCLUDED.` · `PRACTICE AT THE END OF A RAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one task, done fully. Settle and let the breath come and go. Pick a small piece of work from today, one you were going to rush. Washing a cup. Answering one email. Folding one shirt. Run it through slowly in your mind, from the first touch to the last. Notice the moment you usually start thinking about the next thing, and stay with this one instead. If you can, get up afterward and actually do it, start to finish, with nothing else in your hands. The bell holds the time.
Baizhang's rake. The old Chan teacher who kept working in the fields, and went without food when his tools were hidden. Today's word.
Your line: no work, no food. Today, before you eat one meal, do one piece of today's work fully, even if it's small, and notice how the food tastes after it. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: In Zen and Chan monasteries, daily work called samu (in Japanese) is part of the schedule: residents and teachers share cleaning, cooking and garden work as practice, alongside sitting and chanting.

fork.setup: you're the old teacher. you wake up and your tools are gone; the monks hid them so you'd rest. what do you do?
options: scold the monks and demand them back
fork.reveal: Baizhang didn't scold anyone. he just didn't eat: a day without work is a day without food. the monks gave the tools back.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strict old man's rule about earning your dinner.
what it means: Baizhang treated the day's work as part of his own practice, and would not let others take it from him.
what a scholar hears: tradition credits Baizhang with the Chan monastic code, though how much of the written code goes back to him is uncertain.
